771.title: Draupadi's question
771.hook: Draupadi asks the elders to their faces, and Bhishma answers: the ways of dharma are subtle
771.carry: the ways of dharma are subtle
771.howItsDone: Bhishma's reply that dharma is subtle is quoted and debated by Hindu teachers and readers as a picture of how hard right action can be, and of what silence costs.

segments.voice: Yesterday a messenger carried Draupadi's question back and forth: which had Yudhishthira lost first, himself or her? And he said nothing.

This part of the story is hard, and i'll tell it plainly and with care. Duhshasana goes to the women's rooms. Draupadi tries to get away, and he seizes her by the hair and drags her into the assembly. The telling says she's in a single garment, and in distress. Here's what stands out about her, in a hall full of men who have just watched her gambled away. She doesn't only cry out. She argues.
screen: `A HARD SCENE, TOLD WITH CARE.` → `DRAGGED INTO THE HALL.` → `SHE ARGUES.`

segments.voice: She looks at the elders and asks how they can sit and watch this. Where has the dharma of these kings gone, she asks, if they can see this done and stay silent? Then, plainly: was I won, or not? Answer it. Bhishma answers. What he says is honest in its way, and painful. The ways of dharma are subtle, he says. One who owns nothing can't stake what belongs to another. And yet a wife, as the custom of the time held, is under her husband's authority. Holding both, he says he can't settle it. He adds that Yudhishthira himself admits he was beaten, and that Shakuni is a master at dice. The question has gone up to the eldest, and the eldest has set it down again, unsettled. Draupadi answers him sharply. Yudhishthira was called to the game, she says, by players skilled and crooked, and he had no skill at it himself. How can anyone say he played by free choice? Some readers hear Bhishma's answer as cowardice. Others hear an old man caught between two rules, refusing to pretend the knot is simple. The poem doesn't decide that for us. What it does show is this: when the person with the most authority in the room says it's subtle, the person who pays for that subtlety is still standing in the middle of the hall, waiting.
screen: `WHERE IS THE DHARMA OF THESE KINGS?` · `BHISHMA: THE WAYS OF DHARMA ARE SUBTLE.` · `TWO RULES, AND NO VERDICT.` · `HE DIDN'T CHOOSE TO PLAY.` · then, large: `SHE IS STILL WAITING.`

772.title: Draupadi's question
772.hook: Bhima answers with fire, Arjuna holds him back, and Vikarna, a Kaurava, answers with reasons
772.howItsDone: Vikarna is remembered in retellings as the Kaurava who spoke for Draupadi, and Arjuna's restraint of Bhima is told as a moment when the brothers refused to turn on each other.

segments.voice: Yesterday Bhishma said the ways of dharma are subtle, and left Draupadi's question unsettled while she stood waiting.

Two voices break the silence, and they break it in opposite directions. First Bhima. He has watched his eldest brother stake him, lose him, and then lose Draupadi, and his anger has nowhere to go. In the telling, he turns it on Yudhishthira himself. Then someone nobody expects speaks up, a young man from the other side of the family. Two answers to Draupadi's question: one made of fury, one made of reasons.
screen: `TWO VOICES BREAK THE SILENCE.` → `ONE WITH FURY.` → `ONE WITH REASONS.`

segments.voice: Bhima's words are shocking. Gamblers, he says, don't stake even the women kept in their houses. Then he turns to Sahadeva: bring fire, and I'll burn this brother's arms. It's the rage of someone who loves his brother and can't bear what his brother has done. Arjuna stops him. In effect he says: our enemies want exactly this, to see us turn on our eldest. Yudhishthira was challenged, and he kept a warrior's custom. And Bhima holds back. Then Vikarna speaks. He's one of Duryodhana's own brothers, a Kaurava, and he stands up in his family's hall and says: answer her. Nobody does. So he answers it himself, with reasons. Kings, he says, are prone to certain vices: hunting, drinking, dice, and too much pleasure. A man in the grip of one of them acts without judgment. Yudhishthira staked Draupadi in the grip of the game, and only when Shakuni prompted him. He had already lost himself. And she's the wife of all five brothers, not his alone. For these reasons, Vikarna says, she was not won. The hall erupts. Voices across the hall cheer him and blame Shakuni. For a moment it looks as if the question has an answer. Notice who gave it: not an elder, not a Pandava, but a younger brother of the winning side, willing to say the unwelcome thing to his own family.

773.title: Draupadi's question
773.hook: Karna answers Vikarna, an order is given, and the cloth keeps coming
773.howItsDone: The unending cloth is told in homes, sung in devotional songs and danced on stage; devotees see in it Krishna's protection of one who calls on him.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vikarna, a Kaurava, answered Draupadi's question with reasons: she was not won. And the hall cheered.

The cheering for Vikarna doesn't last. Karna rises, Duryodhana's friend, and he's angry. He doesn't simply shout, the way Bhima did a moment ago. He comes at it with arguments of his own, point after point, aimed straight at the young man who dared to speak for her. Then, briefly and with care: what the hall tries to do to Draupadi, and what it can't do.
screen: `THE CHEERING DOESN'T LAST.` → `KARNA RISES.` → `AN ANSWER TO THE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Karna tells Vikarna he's a boy talking like an elder. The elders, he says, have kept quiet, and that means they think she was won. Yudhishthira staked everything he owned, and Draupadi was part of everything. He named her in plain words, and the Pandavas let it happen. Then Karna says cruel things about Draupadi herself, insults meant to make her less than a wife, and i won't repeat them. He orders Duhshasana: take the Pandavas' upper garments, and Draupadi's too. The Pandavas take off their upper cloths and sit down. Duhshasana seizes Draupadi's garment and begins to pull. Here the telling becomes a wonder. Draupadi cries out, and in Ganguli's telling she calls on Krishna by name. As Duhshasana pulls, another garment appears beneath, and another, of many colors, until a great heap lies on the floor, and he sinks down, worn out and ashamed. Karna's arguments didn't answer Draupadi's question. They tried to make it unnecessary, by making her less than a person who could ask one. The wonder answers that in its own way: however much is pulled away, she isn't uncovered. Then Bhima, shaking with rage, swears before everyone that one day, in battle, he'll drink Duhshasana's blood. The hall shudders. The question is still standing, and so is she.

774.title: Draupadi's question
774.hook: Vidura tells the hall of Prahlada, a father who judged against his own son rather than answer falsely
774.carry: staying silent shares in the wrong
774.howItsDone: Vidura's story of Prahlada's honest verdict is retold as a lesson about speaking truly in a council.

segments.voice: Yesterday Karna argued from the elders' silence, and the cloth kept coming. She is still standing.

The heap of cloth lies on the floor. The hall is shaken, and still no one has answered Draupadi. So Vidura stands, and instead of an argument, he tells an old story. It's about a judge asked to decide a case in which his own son was one of the two sides. The question for him was simple and terrible: will you tell the truth if it costs your own child?
screen: `STILL NO ONE HAS ANSWERED.` → `VIDURA TELLS A STORY.` → `A JUDGE, AND HIS OWN SON.`

segments.voice: Vidura begins with the hall. Draupadi has asked a question, he says, and it must be answered. Someone who knows the answer and stays silent shares in the wrong, and so does someone who answers falsely. Then the story. Two young men, Virochana, Prahlada's son, and Sudhanvan, a Brahmin's son, quarreled over which of them was the greater, and staked their lives on it. They went to Prahlada, Virochana's own father, to judge between them. Sudhanvan warned him: answer falsely, or not at all, and you'll suffer for it. Troubled, Prahlada went to the sage Kashyapa and asked what becomes of one who won't answer, or who answers wrongly. Kashyapa told him such a person carries a heavy burden of wrong. So Prahlada came back and gave his verdict, against his own son. Sudhanvan is the greater, he said, and Sudhanvan's father is greater than I am. And Sudhanvan, moved by that honesty, gave Virochana's life back to his father. Then Vidura turns to the kings and elders and says, in effect: you've heard it. Now think, and answer her. Prahlada had every reason to tilt the truth: it was his own son. He didn't. The kings in the hall have far less at stake, and still they won't speak. The telling says that even after Vidura's story, the kings said nothing at all.
screen: `VIDURA: SILENCE SHARES IN THE WRONG.` · `TWO YOUNG MEN, ONE QUARREL.` · `PRAHLADA JUDGES AGAINST HIS SON.` · `STILL THE KINGS SAY NOTHING.` · then, large: `ANSWER HER.`

775.title: Draupadi's question
775.hook: the question is never answered, but omens frighten the blind king, and Draupadi frees her husbands with two boons
775.howItsDone: Draupadi's two boons and her refusal of a third are retold as a sign of her dignity and judgment, and in parts of south India Draupadi herself is honored as a goddess.

segments.voice: Yesterday Vidura told of Prahlada, who judged against his own son, and still no one answered Draupadi. Staying silent shares in the wrong.

Draupadi asks one more time. In the telling, she says she has been dragged here and wronged before everyone, and still no one has spoken. Then, once more: am I a slave, or free? Say it, and I'll accept it. And this time something does answer, though not from the people in the hall. By the end of this long day, a blind king finally speaks.

Bhishma answers once more, and again he can't settle it: Yudhishthira alone, he says, should say whether she was won. Duryodhana, smiling, picks up that idea. Let the four younger brothers say Yudhishthira wasn't their master, and she'll be free. A trap, set in front of everyone. Before the brothers answer, Duryodhana makes an insulting gesture toward Draupadi, and Bhima swears a second vow, against Duryodhana. Then Arjuna answers the trap: Yudhishthira was our master when he staked us, but whose master was he once he'd lost himself? Then the sounds begin. In the telling, a jackal howls in the chamber where the king's sacred fire is kept. Donkeys bray. Birds cry out on every side. Gandhari hears it. Vidura hears it. They tell the blind king. And Dhritarashtra, frightened, finally acts. He rebukes his son, and offers Draupadi a boon. She asks for Yudhishthira's freedom, so that her son won't be called a slave's son. Granted. He offers a second. She asks that the other four go free, with their weapons and chariots. Granted. Then he offers a third, and Draupadi refuses. A woman of a warrior's house, she says, may ask two boons and no more; her husbands, now free, can win the rest by their own deeds. Her question was never answered, not by Bhishma, not by the kings. Yet by the end of the day, it was her asking, not any argument made in that hall, that set five brothers free.

776.title: Vana: exile
776.hook: a second game, a stake of forest and hiding, and the people of the city follow the Pandavas out
776.carry: take one breath on the threshold
776.howItsDone: The Vana Parva, the book of the forest, is read and retold for the many stories the Pandavas hear during their exile.

segments.voice: Yesterday Draupadi's question went unanswered to the end, yet with two boons, and no third, she freed five brothers.

The Pandavas set out for home, free, with their weapons and their chariots. They don't get far. Back in the hall, Duryodhana is already talking to his father. In the telling, a messenger catches up with Yudhishthira on the road and calls him back for one more game. The stake this time isn't gold or brothers. It's exile. The book of the hall closes, and the long book of the forest, the Vana, begins.
screen: `FREE, AND ON THE ROAD.` → `CALLED BACK FOR ONE MORE GAME.` → `THE BOOK OF THE FOREST BEGINS.`

segments.voice: Yudhishthira hears the summons, and he turns around. In the telling, he says that good and evil come to beings as the creator ordains, whether he plays or not, and that, summoned by the old king, he won't refuse. The terms are set. Whoever loses goes into the forest for twelve years, dressed in deer skins, then spends a thirteenth year in some town without being recognized. If they're recognized in that last year, it begins again: another twelve. Shakuni throws, and wins. So the Pandavas take off their royal clothes and put on deer skins. As they leave, the poem gives each of them a gesture, described to the blind king by Vidura. Yudhishthira covers his face. Bhima looks at his great arms. Arjuna scatters sand as he walks. The twins smear themselves with dust. Draupadi goes weeping, her face covered by her loosened hair. Their mother Kunti stays behind in Vidura's house. Then, as the Vana Parva opens, something unexpected: the people of the city follow them out. They won't stay in a city ruled by those who did this. Yudhishthira has to turn and ask them, gently, to go home. Vana means forest. In this story it's a place of loss, and also where the brothers will hear much teaching: sages, stories inside stories, hard questions beside a lake. But that's ahead. Today is the first step off the road and under the trees.
screen: `CALLED BACK, HE DOESN'T REFUSE.` · `THE STAKE: FOREST, THEN HIDING.` · `DEER SKINS, DUST AND LOOSENED HAIR.` · `THE CITY FOLLOWS THEM OUT.` · then, large: `UNDER THE TREES.`

777.title: Vana: exile
777.hook: the Brahmanas follow the exiles into the forest, and Yudhishthira has nothing to feed them until the sun gives a vessel
777.howItsDone: The story of Surya's vessel is retold in Hindu storytelling, and Draupadi's serving of guests in the forest is remembered alongside the tradition's high regard for hospitality to guests.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Vana, the forest. The Pandavas left the city in deer skins, and the people followed them out. Your line was take one breath on the threshold.

A crowd is following the exiles. The Pandavas have lost their kingdom, their wealth and their palace, and still a company of Brahmanas keeps walking behind them into the trees, refusing to turn back. That night, by the water, Yudhishthira lies awake with a very practical problem. He can't send his guests away; a host doesn't do that. And he has nothing to feed them. How do you feed the people who chose to stay?
screen: `A CROWD FOLLOWS THE EXILES.` → `NOTHING TO FEED THEM.` → `HOW DO YOU FEED THOSE WHO STAY?`

segments.voice: The family priest, Dhaumya, gives him counsel. Turn to Surya, the sun, he says: it is the sun that ripens what the earth gives, and so feeds every creature. So Yudhishthira purifies himself, stands in the water, and praises the sun by name after name. And Surya appears, blazing, with a gift: a copper vessel. Whatever food is cooked in your kitchen, the sun tells him, will not run out for your guests, as long as Draupadi has not yet eaten. So the forest household finds its shape. Draupadi serves the Brahmanas first. Then her husbands. Only after everyone else has eaten does she eat, and only then is the vessel empty for the day. Think about what kind of gift this is. Not a palace, or an army, or a way home. It's a way to keep being a host in a place where they own nothing. Exile doesn't stop the Pandavas from feeding people; it turns their camp into a table. And the whole gift turns on Draupadi. Earlier this week, in our telling, she stood in a hall where no one would answer her. Here, the household lives by her timing. So the week holds two pictures side by side: in the hall, a question left hanging; in the forest, a woman serving everyone before herself, with a vessel from the sun in her hands.
screen: `DHAUMYA: TURN TO THE SUN.` · `A COPPER VESSEL FROM SURYA.` · `FOOD LASTS UNTIL DRAUPADI EATS.` · then, large: `THE CAMP BECOMES A TABLE.`

segments.voice: Picture a table you've sat at: a kitchen, a cafeteria, a friend's floor with takeout boxes, and see who did the serving and who ate last. Breathe in what was given to you there, and breathe out a little gratitude toward whoever kept that table going. If you pray, give thanks for your food in your own words or with a line from your own tradition; if not, simply stay with the faces at that table.
